solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: They help one see exact requirements

blocks.note: first meaning: informal word for spectacles, the glasses you wear
second meaning: short for specifications, the detailed requirements of a job

explanation.surface: Someone praising tools or guides that make exact requirements clear.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one sentence, but it splits into two separate meanings of the same short informal word.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasses are informally called by this word, and it is also the clipped form of specifications in technical writing.

clue.text: More than one problem for the auditor

indicators.note: an auditor here is a listener, so what follows is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem, as set in school

explanation.surface: An accountant's auditor finding more than one problem in the books.
explanation.walkthrough: The auditor looks like the financial inspector of the surface, but here the word means a hearer; SUM and SOME sound identical.
explanation.definitionFit: The determiner refers to an unspecified quantity greater than a single item, as in 'some apples'.

clue.text: For peace of mind, stop leaving Charlie out

indicators.note: to leave something out is to omit it, so a letter is dropped from the word

blocks.note: to cease is to stop
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Advice to stop excluding a friend called Charlie if you want a clear conscience.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie looks like a person being left out of the group, but he is just the letter C removed from CEASE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ease is a state of calm free from worry or anxiety, which is a synonym for having peace of mind.

clue.text: Revised content of book appears in TV programme

indicators.note: the content of something is what lies inside it, so only the inner letters are kept
a revised text has been altered and rearranged, so the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: the two middle letters of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: An edited version of a book's content being shown on television.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a book adaptation; instead the inner letters of 'book' join 'appears' and are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: A soap opera is a long-running serial drama broadcast on television, so it is one kind of TV programme.

clue.text: Source of information beginning to embarrass Secret Intelligence Service

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter is kept

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information
first letter of the word
SIS is the abbreviation for the Secret Intelligence Service, Britain's MI6

explanation.surface: A leak from a spy source that threatens to embarrass MI6.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Source of information' reads as one phrase, but the definition is only 'Source'; GEN is British slang for facts or info.
explanation.definitionFit: A genesis is the origin or starting point of something, so it is a synonym for source.

clue.text: Chap that lets off steam on the radio

indicators.note: radio is heard rather than seen, so the word is taken by its spoken sound

blocks.note: a geyser is a hot spring that shoots out steam

explanation.surface: A man who rants and vents his frustration on a radio phone-in.
explanation.walkthrough: Letting off steam suggests an angry caller, but it is a literal description of a hot spring. The British pronunciation of GEYSER is needed for the sound match.
explanation.definitionFit: Geezer is British informal slang for a man or bloke, so it matches chap as a casual word for a fellow.

clue.text: Pin-up shot

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: taken as written; that the whole of 'Pin-up' also contains the reversed letters is a coincidence of the hyphenated form

explanation.surface: A photograph of a pin-up model.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen glues 'Pin-up' into a glamour poster, but it splits into a word and its reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A nip is a small measure of spirits, the same as a shot of whisky or similar drink.

clue.text: University in Bern soon rebuilt

indicators.note: something rebuilt is put together again in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Swiss university in Bern that is due to be reconstructed shortly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface places the university in Switzerland, but the famous one is in Paris; Bern is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sorbonne is the historic university in Paris, a well-known example of a seat of higher learning.

clue.text: In state of shock, began to grab line

indicators.note: to grab something is to take hold of it, so one piece closes around another

blocks.note: to start is to begin
L is the standard abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: Someone in shock instinctively reaching for a rope or line to hold.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an adjectival phrase at the start; STARTED wraps round L.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone startled has been suddenly surprised or alarmed, which describes being in a state of shock.

clue.text: Somehow makes it slip

indicators.note: somehow means in some unknown way, so the letters come out in some unstated order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something mysteriously causing an object to slide out of place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slip' reads as a verb in the surface, but it is the noun meaning an error.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip is a small error or oversight, so it is a synonym for a mistake made by accident.

clue.text: Soldier nicking £1000 coat

indicators.note: to nick is to steal, and what is stolen is taken inside, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: a para is a paratrooper
K stands for a thousand, as in a £10K salary

explanation.surface: A soldier caught stealing a thousand-pound coat.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick is British slang for steal. PARA, short for paratrooper, takes K inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A parka is a hooded, padded jacket for cold weather, so it is a kind of coat.

clue.text: The orator’s curious complaint

indicators.note: curious can mean odd or strange, so the letters are arranged in a peculiar way

blocks.note: taken as written, including the s after the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A public speaker with a strange grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'complaint' a grievance, but here it is a minor ailment; a speaker is just the person likely to suffer one.
explanation.definitionFit: Complaint can mean a minor illness or ailment, and an inflamed, painful throat is a common example.

clue.text: Attack and eat a ruminant

blocks.note: to have a meal is to eat it
taken as written
a goat is a cud-chewing animal

explanation.surface: A predator pouncing on and devouring a grazing animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one predatory act, but 'Attack' is the definition and 'and' just joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a go at someone is a British idiom for criticising or assaulting them, verbally or physically.

clue.text: Important company directors enter data with this?

definitions.note: a description of the thing, standing for the noun

blocks.note: key means crucial or important
a company's directors form its board

explanation.surface: Senior executives typing figures into a computer themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description ending in a question mark: what you type data in with.
explanation.definitionFit: Typing on a computer's set of keys is the usual way to input information, so the device fits the description.

clue.text: Important date in boring profession

blocks.note: a dead place or party is dull and boring
one's line is one's line of work, a profession

explanation.surface: A key day in the career of someone with a dull job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like it should put something inside something else, but it only joins definition to wordplay. 'Boring' is not drilling here but dull.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadline is the fixed time by which work must be finished, a date that matters greatly.

clue.text: A number accommodated in hotel eventually

indicators.note: to be accommodated in a place is to be lodged inside it, so the letters sit within the words

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A group of guests finally finding rooms at a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A number' sounds like a quantity of guests being housed, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleven is the integer after ten, one specific example of a number.

clue.text: Tree-lined street, a place for musicians to perform

blocks.note: taken as written
a concert hall or club where a gig is held

explanation.surface: A leafy street that doubles as a spot for street musicians to play.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma separates two descriptions that seem to describe one place; the second simply splits into A and VENUE.
explanation.definitionFit: An avenue is a broad road, traditionally one bordered by rows of trees on both sides.

clue.text: Job Elizabeth II performed dutifully at first

indicators.note: at first points to the opening position, so only the initial letter is taken

blocks.note: Elizabeth Regina, the royal cipher of the late Queen
to run an event or a show is to perform or conduct it
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: The late Queen carrying out a task with characteristic sense of duty.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, for Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's cipher seen on postboxes. 'Performed' gives RAN as in ran a race.
explanation.definitionFit: An errand is a short trip to do a task for someone, a small job such as fetching shopping.

clue.text: Occasion giving you a terrible shock?

definitions.text: Occasion giving you a terrible shock?

blocks.clueFragment: Occasion giving you a terrible shock?
blocks.note: surface reading: an event that gives you a nasty fright
setter's reading: a shock is a thick mass of hair, so a day when your hair looks awful

explanation.surface: An event that leaves you badly frightened.
explanation.walkthrough: Shock looks like a fright, but it also means a bushy head of hair, as in 'a shock of red hair'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a day when your hair will not behave, extended to any day when things go wrong.

clue.text: School register returned

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to note is to register or take notice of

explanation.surface: A school's attendance register being handed back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'register' looks like the noun, a class roll, but it is the verb meaning to take note. Eton is a famous English private school.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton College is the well-known English boarding school near Windsor, one example of a school.

clue.text: Prospective MP wants this car

blocks.note: first meaning: a constituency place in Parliament, which a candidate hopes to win
second meaning: a Spanish car manufacturer

explanation.surface: A parliamentary candidate with their eye on a particular car.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one wish, but splits into a description of a parliamentary place and a car brand.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of Parliament win constituencies, called seats, and SEAT is also a Spanish make of motor vehicle.

clue.text: Sign of tooth decay initially ignored

indicators.note: the initial letter is the first one, and ignoring it means leaving it off

blocks.note: caries is the medical term for tooth decay

explanation.surface: An early warning of a cavity that the patient overlooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign of tooth decay' looks like a symptom, but 'Sign' is a star sign and 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Aries, the Ram, is the first of the twelve zodiac signs used in astrology.

clue.text: Reportedly catch sight of ocean

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so its sound is what counts

blocks.note: to catch sight of something is to see it

explanation.surface: A traveller said to have glimpsed the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: SEE and SEA are pronounced the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea and ocean both name a large body of salt water, so they are near-synonyms.

clue.text: Maybe bitter about situation, as Peter was?

definitions.note: a description of the thing, standing for the noun

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is wrapped around another

blocks.note: bitter is a type of beer, an ale; 'Maybe' marks it as an example
a post is a job or position

explanation.surface: Someone resentful about their circumstances, like Peter after his denial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bitter' reads as resentful, but bitter is a British pale beer. The definition is the closing phrase about Saint Peter.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Peter was one of the twelve disciples chosen by Jesus to spread his teaching.

clue.text: Film that is tough on daughter

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter
i.e. is the Latin abbreviation id est, that is
hard means tough

explanation.surface: A movie that treats a daughter harshly.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue, 'on' puts the earlier pieces after the daughter, so D comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Die Hard is the 1988 action movie starring Bruce Willis, a famous example of a film.

clue.text: An article of faith, one way or another

indicators.note: either way you read it you get the same thing, so the letters run identically in both directions

blocks.note: a core belief held by a religion

explanation.surface: A belief held by one religion or another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one way or another' sounds like a vague phrase about religions, but it says the word reads the same forwards and backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenet is a principle or doctrine held as true, such as a belief taught by a church.
